image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Bubble chart / scatter plot**
- Bubbles are plotted along a horizontal percentage scale and sized by industry sales.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
- **Color grouping** separates categories into two groups (orange vs. teal)
- **Bubble size encoding** is used to show magnitude
- Points appear **jittered vertically** for separation; the vertical position does not show a labeled quantitative axis
- No stacking

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in spending from 2019 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis (percentage from negative to positive) |
| Industry sales | Quantitative | Bubble area/size |
| Industry / merchant category | Categorical/nominal | Text labels attached to selected bubbles |
| Spending direction/group | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (orange for less spending side, teal for more spending side) |

If useful, I can also provide a plain-language summary of the main visual pattern.

We’ve all faced an issue of having to choose to spend on one item versus another. Maybe it was the new video game you’ve wanted, or a movie night out with your friends. Most of the time we can’t do it all so we have to be smart with our money. Well this pandemic has brought frugal spending to a whole other degree. With people out of work and no steady income, there has to be prioritizing of our wants and needs. We’re forced to take better care of our money and spend it on essential goods, not the luxuries like movie theater and cruises pictured.

Were able to see the shift in consumer spending, but what we were not able to see is its impacts on small business owners. Points on the graph that have increased belong to large companies and corporations. Those who work for and own the large companies are doing better off with the increase in consumer spending, while small business owners are forced to close for the time being, and many will never reopen. 

We fear what we don’t know, and right now the future is unpredictable. How will this virus change the way our businesses run in the future? How will it affect our little beach town tourist season with it being a large economic boost?

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that people are spending more money on activities that can be done indoors or at home, such as gaming. Additionally, spending on necessities such as groceries and other food items (e.g. meal kits) has increased dramatically. This is feasible since more people are confined to their homes and cannot eat at restaurants or partake in leisurely activities outside. On another note, I wonder why charitable giving has gone down... I initially thought that spending on charity would increase, because people would want to help those less fortunate than themselves during this crisis. However, it appears as though people are putting their own needs first instead of considering those of others in worse situations. In this way, the graph also serves as an interesting analysis on human behavior- while spending on streaming and video games have gone up, charity has decreased. For this reason, a catchy name for the graph could be "Covid Spending: Self Over Sacrifice." This is a time when we should be helping others, which should be highlighted over consumer purchases.

comments.raw_comment:
I live in a beach city on the coast of North Carolina that thrives off of the tourist industry. This reveal has made me wonder more about people locally than people nationally and globally. Many people in my town depend on travelers; many people own and work at beach-front and historic downtown/river-front restaurants and stores. Even though we have few cases (when compared to some other states), I can't help but be concerned for most of the people in my community. What will their lives look like in the next year, without tourists, and probably without as many local customers as they've had in the past?

I also wonder about the net effect of COVID buying habits on a small and large scale after reading the Stat Nuggets. The net effect is altogether negative, meaning that most purchases are in decline, with a few exceptions. However, some areas are inevitably more or less affected than others; New York will be more affected than Montana, obviously, but what about places around North Carolina? What about small towns with little to no cases of COVID? What about cities that have many people working like normal (just from home instead), or make a large number of online sales? I suspect some people/areas will benefit from our COVID chaos while others definitely don't, but either way, the net effect will be what affects all of us for the months (years?) to come. It'll be interesting to see what happens, locally, nationally, and globally.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that more industries are taking hits in how much money people spend on them instead of gains. Upon closer observation one can see how mostly all the struggling industries are all entertainment industries, more specifically industries that get most of their revenue from  mostly middle class people. This could be due to the fact that many people of this  status are the people who have enough money to spend on entertainment things, but are not extremely wealthy, so are now being very precautions in spendings on non necessities. Another important factor that I noticed was that many of the industries that are going below what they made last year usually flourish in this spring summer portion of the year, such as cruses, and air lines. With these declines being in their busiest months it could be even more costly to them.

I wonder… It is interesting to me that the amount of money spent on charity has gone down in trying times like these and honestly quite saddening, but again it is most likely due to people frugalness in these times where our economy is in flux and people do not know if they will come out of this economically sound. Another interesting statistic is that the home improvements industry seems to have gained around 15%-20% more income than last year, and this is so interesting because it seems to be a luxury to do home improvements, but people are not shying away from spending money on that sort of thing. 

-Caroline Keohane 8th grade

After reading the Reveal, I noticed first that the data pool was relatively low. While 6 million people surveyed sounds like a lot, compared to the roughly 328 million people in the US, it's a small data pool. Some people during this pandemic probably aren't even buying very much anyway. This graph doesn't show those people either. It doesn't show how people are saving money during this time. It just implies that instead of splurging on airplane tickets, they're splurging on video games. 

One thing that this graph has showed me is that the economy is changing drastically due to Covid-19. It doesn't show how popular those industries shown were before the virus, so I can't tell if they're on the verge of going bankrupt, but I know that some businesses will and already have gone bankrupt. If enough places go out of business, our spending habits could permanently change.

Maybe Covid-19 just accelerated some of the processes that were going to happen anyway. Technology is growing increasingly popular, so maybe the increase in video game sales might have gone up anyway. Maybe some of the small businesses were doomed to fail anyway, so maybe some of the changes in sales are less because of Covid-19 and more because of peoples' changing tastes.

The stat nuggets show that with people choosing to adhere to social distancing and self-quarantine suggestions, many of them are choosing to shop for their groceries online instead of in person. At the same time, it highlights the ease and familiarity that supermarkets pose for people who want to get all their necessities and food at one time and only have to go out once in a few weeks. This shows the peril that some small grocery stores are feeling when there are fewer customers who go there instead of large wholesale stores like Costco (if the entire family is staying home, people might need to get larger packs of everything that are sold in those wholesale stores).

I think that this graph was really nice. It showed the actions and mindset of many people who are spending time at home because of Covid-19. It also effectively shows the different priorities, from stocking up on their favorite alcohol to buying methods of entertainment like video games.

After reading the reveal, I can’t say it doesn’t make sense. Of course in a global pandemic the sales from movie theaters, restaurants, gyms, and cruises would decline. Naturally, with the stay-at-home orders, there would be an increase in sales for gaming and online groceries, granted, as explained in the stat nuggets, those industries are still relatively small. 

Although opening businesses up too early may be a fatal mistake, it is impossible to stay closed for such a long period of time. The graph clearly shows that people aren’t spending their money on local business, and those stores are feeling the repercussions of that. It makes sense that people aren’t going to their local barber shop or brick and mortar shop. It makes sense general merchandise and ecommerce is a significantly larger bubble than fitness

Although the reveal provided a great deal of information that made the graph more understandable, I still left wondering whose spending was tracked in this. Was it the wealthy in the gated community or the local businessman who just went bankrupt? Six million people is a large study group, but does it represent the wide diversity of wealth and status that exists in America? Does this study truly represent all the different walks of life in America?

comments.raw_comment: This graph shows how the coronavirus outbreak has affected our spending habits. Spending has decreased rapidly in airlines, movie theaters, cruises, and lodging, and has also partially decreased in charitable giving and fast food. This makes sense as many of these things require large groups and social interaction, which poses a threat to spreading the disease. However, spending has increased in things like online grocery delivery, gaming, e-commerce, and supermarkets. This also makes sense as this spending is more compatible with isolation. I wonder how spending is projected to change once the lockdown is lifted.

I noticed that many things that had very large industry sales have barely moved, which I believe is most likely because they are things people are used to having. For example, supermarkets have barely moved, because people can’t live without food, and thus people who bought food before are still buying food now. Also, despite the fact that people have been buying more food at once, people who stock up on food one week might not have to go get food the next week. 

I am wondering about why mobile services have decreased. This doesn’t seem to make much sense, because more people are at home, and have more chances to buy things on their phones.

comments.raw_comment:
When I look at this graph for the third time this week, I am reminded of how much your vision and perspective towards an image or piece of writing can change over time. Now, as I glance at this graph, I wonder how the colors and sizes of each dot play a role- as if the red circles on the left side of the graph are instantly associated with something negative, while the green circles on the right side of the graph are instantly associated with something positive. It's compelling that our brains may make this type of association subconsciously. 

I noticed something that I hadn't before today, warehouse clubs, places where you can buy large quantities of food in bulk, are still receiving the same amount of revenue that they were before the pandemic. This makes me contemplate, why aren't people choosing to buy in bulk? Especially now, when grocery stores are jam packed and supplies are running low? Rather, it seems that more people are interested in grocery stores delivering and purchasing meal kits. On some level, this makes sense, but personally, I would think that people would want to buy copious amounts of food and supplies during a time like this, just in case. 

 I expect that for the most part, the spending habits will remain relatively the same for all humans until this comes to an end. 
My final catchy headline that I think best represents what I see today is: Looking at Spending Habits From a Distance.

comments.raw_comment:
As suspected, social distancing is playing a significant role in how the average American spends their money.  After reading the Stat Nugget, I learned that many industries are struggling like Brick and mortar stores, dine-in restaurants, and travel agencies and have lost 50% or more of regular sales. It puts the virus in perspective as not only threatening our health, but threatening our economy, jobs, and potentially our way of life. 

When I first looked at the graph, I knew it was terrible that some major industries were plummeting. After the reveal, I realize the incredible impact of these industries. Food, travel, and transportation industries provide tons of jobs to keep the economy healthy. Most of them have fallen past 50%, and about 16 million workers have filed unemployment because of the virus.

 I believe that this graph is saying if we don't begin to salvage these "pillars of American Industry," we are going to suffer heavy losses in the economy. Coronavirus seems to be the only thing on everyone's mind, and staying safe is the number one priority. Still, the economy is slowly spiraling, and we need to try to get back to the standard way of life to save both American's health and wealth.

comments.raw_comment:
One thing I noticed was the ratio of bubbles on the left to the one on the right. Since these bubbles represent industries and the percentage of spending that is being made towards those industries it’s clear to see that there are more industries that have suffered from the isolation of society to those that have gained. Many of these industries are related to or involve traveling (seen in Airline, Cruises and lodging) or social interaction and usage of a communal area (seen in Movie theaters, Fast food, Fitness and charitable giving). 
Meanwhile on the right we can see industries that can thrive through online interactions, gaming or delivery services as people become less willing to go outside.
Some industries are surprising to see where they are on the graph. I expected mobile to actually be used more since people would spend more time calling mother but I suppose that when you're in the confines of your home there are other methods than calling and cellular data wouldn’t be needed since there’s internet service. Another strange one is Home improvement. You’d think letting a stranger in your house to fix it while in quarantine from a virus would be the last thing one would want to do, so I wonder if there’s another way that that industry is growing, as well as why people are suddenly investing in the improvement of their homes. 
I was thinking about the phrase “ in a nutshell” except this time with bubble. So a name for this would be Industry Inside a Bubble.

comments.raw_comment:
"Priority Shift"

I noticed that although we obviously are not spending money on travel and vacationing, the spending before and after the effects of Covid-19 are still mainly entertainment and food. These spending habits also show how we are observing social distancing and various stay-at-home orders. 

There used to be a lot of spending towards entertainment activities that require going out like movie theaters, fitness, transportation, and lodging. Now, money is spent towards at-home entertainment like video games and streaming services. This graph gives evidence on what people spend their time doing (drinking their fill and taking the time to remodel the backyard to one that they’ve always wanted to have).

I wonder if this would change spending habits in the future. People could find new hobbies that they would be willing to invest in or realize that something they used to spend money on isn’t such a necessity anymore.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  "In Is the New Out" by Judy of Las Vegas, “Coronavirus Spending... More or Less?” by Ms. Anderson’s students of Pine Street School in New York City, "Online Industries Dominate during the Pandemic" by Renata of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, New Jersey, and “Covid Troubles & Fiscal Bubbles: How Covid-19 Changed Our Spending Habits“  by Dr. Aiyer ‘s class at The Harker School in San Jose, California.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow -- Thursday afternoon, April 23 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

The next graph will be released in two days -- Friday, April 24, with moderation on Wednesday, April 29.  You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to “What's Going On In This Graph?”  The topic is record-breaking global temperatures in 2019.

You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage.  Or, go to our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph.

The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who has only bought food and made charitable contributions since March 15, and Corey Andreasen, who has been cooking a lot lately.

comments.raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed when looking at the graph was the varying sizes of the bubbles. The ones for general merchandise and e-commerce and supermarkets are huge while the ones for cruises and movie theaters are small. I also noticed how our spending habits seemed to have shifted from luxuries to essential and online items. I wonder what some of the bubbles on the left represent since only a few are labeled. I also wonder how long these changes will last and if it will leave a lasting impact on the industries even after the pandemic is over. 

People are spending more on online grocers, meal kits, and food deliveries but less on fast food. They are spending more on video streaming but less on movie theaters. They are spending more on gaming and less on fitness. Since we can’t go to any of these physical places anymore, it makes sense that people would switch to spending money on their online alternatives. I am curious about the decrease of charitable donations, because although many people are out of a job right now, there are also an increasing number of people who are reliant on donations right now.

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: More or Less Spending Due to the Coronavirus

I notice that there are many more items that people have spent less on than they have spent more on. Due to this national lockdown and pandemic, it has been suggested for people to not leave their houses, except in a case of emergency. Therefore, with this being said, many movie theatres, restaurants, gyms, and airlines have closed. As a result, people have started spending more of their money to improve their homes and to go to supermarkets. Another source of the outcome, is through online purchases, gaming, and other essential goods. 

I wonder what this graph will start to look like once we are further into this lockdown, when even leaving your homes for essentials might be even more dangerous. I am surprised that the buying of masks and latex gloves was not included in the more spending aspect.

This graph displays the data collected on the change of consumer spending's  from March 26 through April 1st 2019 compared to 2020. Covid-19 has greatly influenced the things people are spending their money on today. A catchy headline could be: The Fall of Luxurious Spending.
(I'm not too sure what to categorize the businesses in the less spending section as.)

I noticed from the graph that a lot of things that we regularly would've spent a lot on are on the decreasing side of purchases. Covid-19 has caused people to be trapped in their homes resulting to more spending's via essential supplies, delivery and home oriented things. comments.raw_comment:
Looking at this graph, I immediately noticed that there were more industries with declining than increasing sales. The graph clearly shows how more people are opting to stay inside and save money rather than risk going outside for seemingly "frivolous" things such as fast food, cruises, or movies in theaters. It also seems as though more people are trying to waste as much time on fun or time-consuming activities now that they don't have anywhere to be or anything to do. Looking online during this pandemic, I've seen how people have been picking up more hobbies and doing more busywork, like cleaning or fixing things in their homes.

I wonder if even more people are suffering than would normally be in an outbreak like this due to the decline in charitable giving. Everyone is already suffering, but if those in need before the pandemic are getting even less help now, will they be the ones who don't survive the outbreak? The effect of the pandemic on peoples' money-use could seriously negatively effect the economy in the long run, and I think that prices could end up rising drastically when this is over, just to make up for the break. This could end up driving an even deeper wedge in the wage gap in America.

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: Covid-19 Increases Spending on Home-Centric Goods
        This graph illustrates a shift toward goos that can be used at home. Travel and luxury items like fast food, cruises, and airlines have declined in popularity. Buying things like apparel from brick-and-mortar stores has also dropped. However, sales of things that people can use at home, like video games and alcohol, have gone up. People have been using e-commerce and online grocery shopping more as well. Home improvement sales have had a marked increase also. This increase in purchasing things which can be used at home is likely a result of the coronavirus pandemic.
       When practicing social distancing due to the novel coronavirus, people spend a lot more time at home. When at home, they tend to purchase more house-oriented items, like video games, supplies for home improvement, and alcohol. They also shop online so they do not have to leave the house and risk getting sick. This is likely why e-commerce and online grocery shopping have gone up, while supermarket shopping has stayed the same. Spending on things that are not strictly necessary, like charitable giving and fast food, has gone down. This is probably because of the faltering economy giving people less spare money to donate or spend on fast food. Altogether, there are more things on the decline than the rise. All the decline makes me wonder when the world will pull out of economic decline and all industries will begin to grow again.

comments.raw_comment:
Two days ago when I glanced at the graph shown, I was immediately drawn to the obvious parts of what human beings are globally spending more, and less, money on. Today, I see aspects I neglected to notice before. I noticed that people are spending a significantly less amount of money on vacations (cruises), and fitness. I know that gyms are closed down, along with almost everything else, but this still makes me ponder: are people still finding alternative ways of exercising such as actually going out into nature, or are they just choosing to not be active, for even a small portion of the day at all?

Yes, what's going on in the world right now is terribly troubling. Yes, it's all too exigent to work for home and live life at distance from those who you love the most besides your immediate family. But I think that surely the most efficient way to achieve solace during this time is to practice self-care. Staying healthy by eating wholesome foods and moving by going outside everyday are the best ways to do that. So when I look at this graph, in this moment, and I notice that food delivery and meal kits are at an all time spending popularity high for everyone, I'm happy because that means people are not only supporting businesses and grocery stores in and around their community, but they're in turn also taking care of themselves and their family.

The most fitting headline I can come up with today is- How People are Choosing to Live Through Their Spending Habits.

comments.raw_comment:
In the graph, I noticed that online grocers and gaming is in the lead for more spending, while movie theaters and airlines are almost at 100% less spending. I think online grocers are increasing because people would most likely want to avoid interaction with people at the grocery store, so they would less likely contract the virus, and also prevent spreading it. However, I'm not sure about why gaming has increased sales. I think it has increased because many schools across the U.S. have closed. As an effect, many students learn online and may have more spare time to play video games. 
When looking on the other side of the graph, movie theaters and airlines are some of the things that consumers are spending less on. I think that airlines have less sales for obvious reasons, that they're either closed, people are quarantined, or that no one would like to have a higher risk of contracting the virus. For movie theaters, yet again I'm unsure why its lost more spending than airlines. Movie theaters are a perfect site for spreading the virus, as it occupies a large amount of people. I understand that can cause plenty, if not all theaters to close.
I wonder how the graph will change over the course of the year. I think there will be a significant difference compared to this one.
Headline: The Panic of the Pandemic

comments.raw_comment:
(Part 1)
The first thing to notice on this graph is how overall spending has dropped off from last year. That plus the extreme rise in spending on gaming and streaming services demonstrates how almost everyone is stuck at home, trying to both save money while out of work and entertaining themselves in the midst of a crisis. We can’t go to the gym, we can’t go to movie theaters, we can’t go “non-essential” shopping, and we definitely can’t travel, and even if we legally could, why would we what with the safety concerns and unemployment/financial hardship? The second thing I noticed was the rise of about 25% in spending on alcohol. I can’t help but wonder if this points to high rates of depression and anxiety among people in this time. comments.raw_comment: I notice that this graph shows the change in spending habits in 2019 following the week ending April 1 (this information is shown in the sub-caption under the graph and in the title of the graph). I also notice that the red dots labeled with different industries represent industries with the least spending (less than 0%) and the green dots represent those with the most spending (more than 0%). According to the graph, spending on gaming and online grocers are the highest, while spending on airlines and movie theaters are the lowest. The reason for this is that the most time of the average consumer is now being spent in quarantine, and those staying indoors want food and entertainment without running the risk of leaving the house. The sizing of the dots also represent the industries with the most sales (represented by the sub-caption under the graph). General merchandise and e-commerce as well as supermarkets are receiving the biggest amounts in industry sales in regard to the graph. I wonder why the industries shown to have less spending during this time are more concentrated and greater in number than the industries that are shown to have more spending? Perhaps many of the industries and services provided by those industries rely heavily on outdoor activity. For instance, as travel has been shut down recently, the airline business has been suffering spending-wise. Possible Title: "Online Industries Dominate during the Pandemic."

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released in two days – Friday, April 24 with moderation on Wednesday, April 29.  The topic of the graph – global temperatures.  Stay tuned.

comments.raw_comment:
Title: How We Spend During a Global Pandemic

This graph appears to be measuring two factors, the sales of an industry, represented by the size of the bubble, and whether or not that industry has seen an increase or decrease in spending from the same time a year ago. The number of industries that are in the "red" immediately grabbed my attention, particularly from the airlines and movie theaters, which are experiencing a nearly 100% decrease in spending. 

This graph excellently illuminates the fragility of the global economy. We can group most of the red into entertainment and travel industries, and it's quite astonishing to see how those two industries have led to our economy being left in ruins. It's sad to see charitable giving have such a decrease in their spending, as it leaves thousands struggling on top of the pandemic. 

I was surprised to see supermarkets not experience an increase in spending. I work at a grocery store, and we have seen such an influx of shoppers that we had to start limiting the number of people in the store. Some days it feels like a war zone; the masks, the gloves, the plastic shields at registers. 

I have to wonder what this means for people at home. Since spending is about the same, is food not short in supply? Are people not struggling to find food, or is that even a concern for Americans? This matter gets even more cloudy when we look at the decrease of spending in fast food. Where are those people getting their food, or are they?

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that many of the rises and falls of major industries during the COVID-19 pandemic have balanced out surprisingly well. Major industries, such as movie theaters and airlines, have taken very heavy hits. While movie theaters have been hit severely by the state guidelines in place, streaming services have grown significantly, along with other digital entertainment services, such as gaming. Airlines, which many people previously spent large quantities of money on for vacations  or for business trips, are now not taking as much of people’s money. This money is likely to have been rerouted elsewhere, such as home improvement or alcohol. While seemingly random, the large amounts of money for travel (to entertaining vacations) have been redirected towards home renovations or other at-home pleasure activities. These are the less obvious changes in expenditures, with the more obvious ones being physical purchasing of items such as apparel and food, being swapped for digital or delivery versions of the same services. This shows the forces of supply and demand in the modern market balancing out, even amidst a global crisis. The after-effects of this pandemic will be very interesting to observe later on, especially whether or not major industries that have been affected stay the way they do, or change back to the way they formerly were.

Some things I notice are that there are varying sizes of bubbles, and the bubbles towards the far left and right seem to be more balanced in size in comparison to the middle. The sizes of the bubbles varies more in the middle. The largest bubbles seem to also be the very essential services, such as "supermarkets" and "general merchandise." There are many more bubbles in the "less spending" side than in the "more spending" side. 

I wonder what the "mobile" bubble represents exactly? Is it mobile device spending or mobile as in vehicle mobility/ gas expenses? Something else maybe? 

This graph demonstrates how our spending habits in the U.S. have changed in comparison to the same time last year when COVID-19 was not a threat. Our merchandise and supermarket spending seems to be relatively the same as it was in 2019, but they have increased slightly. Airline ticket, movie theater and cruise spending have decreased by almost 100 percent compared to last year. This makes sense because many people are staying at home, and travelling has been highly discouraged and even banned. Video streaming, food delivery and video game spending (all of which can be no-contact) have all increased by at least 40 percent or more.  A catchy headline would be "Quarantine Is Controlling Your Money."

When I first glanced at the graph shown, I felt a twinge of sadness run through my body as I read everything that people are spending less money on- which entails a lot of small business owners in and around every community across the United States, and across the world. Too many people are loosing or have already lost their jobs and too many people are without food, shelter, or some form of internet to stay educated during this terrifying pandemic. I noticed that getting groceries delivered, video streaming, and purchasing items such as meal kits and alcohol are all things that the general public have been spending increasingly more money on over the past few weeks. Naturally so, people are budgeting their money and prioritizing now, more than ever before. 

I wonder why charitable giving has suddenly decreased in spending by nearly 50%. I fully understand that it's grown to be a lot harder to donate money when money is already scarce for many people. However, for those who don't have any money problems in sight, it frustrates me beyond belief that they wouldn't donate, even if it's the bare minimum, to human beings or a charity in desperate need of basic necessities. In order to support every single person around the world as we all go through such an unimaginable event that will surely make it's mark on global history, we must, collectively do everything in our power to help one another.
The Differentiation of Spending Habits During A Pandemic is my catchy headline.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that many of the rises and falls of major industries during the COVID-19 pandemic have balanced out surprisingly well. Major industries, such as movie theaters and airlines, have taken very heavy hits. While movie theaters have been hit severely by the state guidelines in place, streaming services have grown significantly, along with other digital entertainment services, such as gaming. comments.raw_comment: This graph is only one of the many signs we're seeing so far of capitalism and billion-dollar industries rearing their ugly head in a time of crisis. While it's clear that a vast majority of businesses have seen some bad drops in spending, a majority of said drops being even below -50%, one of the things your eyes are drawn to first on this graph are the massive bubbles of general merchandise/e-commerce and supermarkets. Of course, it is understandable to see that people will be spending more money on these sorts of businesses. I see why these things would make sense of course. And I do not blame people in any way for going and purchasing their needs right now from industries like Amazon and Walmart. But it is just painful to think how businesses that are already always at the top of the food chain are still doing great when many other industries and businesses are struggling, by building themselves off the backs of essential workers. And it's worse when you realize it's all simply a big circle, as it is because these smaller industries and smaller businesses are struggling so much right now, that those of lower class are forced to put themselves and their loved ones at risk working incredibly hard for billion-dollar industries that pay them little to nothing because the system is built in a way that forces them to do so, so that they may give their families food and a roof over their heads. Even in crisis, it is the poor that struggle as the rich grow off their backs.

comments.raw_comment:
During this outbreak, the way we live our lives has fundamentally changed. Not just in how we go to work, or who we see on a daily basis, or when we wake up, but even in how we hold onto our money.
 This is a graph focused on people's spendings- on the profits of different industries in the midst of this chaos Some industries are booming, some industries are failing, others are beyond even that. What I will say, though, is that it all just sort of makes sense. 
 Of course movie theater profits are going down. Of course airlines are making less sales. Of course people aren't going to the gym, instead choosing to work out at home, or just buy more video games and stream more netflix.  Obviously, fewer people are going to get fast food or using their mobile data because few people really have to commute, instead choosing to order food and groceries.
 Everything, down to charitable giving, makes sense. A lot of people are struggling to pay rent right now. It's hard for them to qualify for unemployment checks because of the systems in play. In general, "poorer" people- everyone without a large reserve of money saved for a situation like this- who might've been giving what they could, now can't give anything. Now, at first, I wanted to be disappointed in society for that. I wanted to be angry about "hoarding money" in a time of crisis, but I will concede that its causes make sense, so I really can't fault anyone but those in charge for it.
